name: The sacrifice as the cosmic Person and the world

definitions.definition: The Brāhmaṇas identify the sacrifice with the Person (ŚB 1.3.2.1), with Prajāpati and the year, and with Viṣṇu; the cosmos itself arose from a sacrifice — Brahman offering itself into all beings (ŚB 13.7.1.1), the world-creators' thousand-year session with austerity, truth and breath as priests (TB 3.12.9.3–7) — and the gods live by offering to one another (ŚB 5.1.1.2).

relations.note: the identification is one of the bandhus
the identity of rite, cosmos and person makes an inner rite possible

name: Bandhu — the correspondences between rite, cosmos and person

definitions.definition: The Brāhmaṇas explain every element of a rite by a hidden connection (bandhu) to a cosmic and a bodily counterpart — bricks and days, metres and classes and gods, the breaths and the seers — organized on three planes: of the gods (adhidaivata), of the self (adhyātma) and of the sacrifice (adhiyajña); knowing the connection is what makes the rite work.
Carried into the Āraṇyakas and Upaniṣads as upāsanā — meditations on correspondences (e.g. breath-oblations satisfying senses, gods and regions, ChU 5.19–23; the saṃhitā-upaniṣad, TU 1.3).

name: The three planes: divine, bodily, sacrificial

definitions.definition: Correspondences are drawn in parallel series: in the realm of the gods the sun is the eater and the moon the food; in the realm of the self the breath is the eater and food is its food (ŚB 10.6.2.1–4).
The Āraṇyaka saṃhitā-teachings extend the planes to speech: stops, sibilants and vowels = earth, atmosphere, sky = eye, ear, mind (AA 3.2.5).

name: Prajāpati's falling apart and his restoration

definitions.definition: After emitting the creatures Prajāpati, who is the year, fell apart (vyasraṃsata) — his joints being the junctions of day and night, the moon's phases and the seasons; the gods healed him by the Agnihotra, the new- and full-moon and seasonal rites (ŚB 1.6.3.35–36), and he is rebuilt as the fire-altar whose bricks are his days and nights (ŚB 10.1.1.2–3); he put himself together with the metres, whence 'saṃhitā' (AA 3.2.6).

relations.note: the altar is the means of restoration

notes: Correction to the task wording: the Brāhmaṇas speak of Prajāpati 'coming apart' through the exhaustion of creating, not of a dismemberment by others (contrast the Puruṣa Sūkta, RV 10.90).

name: The year as Prajāpati and as Death

definitions.definition: Prajāpati is the year (saṃvatsara); the Veda's syllables are arranged to equal its moments (ŚB 10.4.2.22–25); the year is also Death, wearing away mortals' lives by days and nights (ŚB 10.4.3.1).
The Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa opens in homage to Prajāpati as lord of the five-year age whose limbs are days, seasons, half-years and months (Ṛk 1).

The great brick altar built over a year in five layers, typically falcon-shaped, sevenfold to a hundred-and-one-fold (ŚB 10.2.3.18); the builder rebuilds Prajāpati, gains immortality after death and escapes re-death (ŚB 10.4.3); its 'secret' (rahasya) in ŚB 10 interiorizes it as fires built of mind, speech, breath, eye, ear and knowledge (ŚB 10.5.3).
Its layout by cord and peg, and the transformation of its shapes with equal area, are the subject of the Śulbasūtras.

Already in the Brāhmaṇas the rite is carried into the person: the self-sacrificer knows each rite builds his own self (ŚB 11.2.6.13); fires are built of mind and knowledge (ŚB 10.5.3); the Agnihotra is 'truth offered in faith' (ŚB 11.3.1.4); feeding brāhmaṇas is 'offering into Brahman' (ĀśGS 1.1.2).
In the Āraṇyakas and Upaniṣads: the inner Agnihotra of speech and breath (KU 2.5), the breath-oblations at meals (ChU 5.19–24), the sacrifice in the body (Prāṇāgnihotra Up.).
The renouncer deposits the sacred fires in himself (MDh 6.38) and the true self-sacrificer sees the self in all beings (MDh 12.91).

relations.note: outer rite and inner rite are two poles of one doctrine

name: Prāṇāgnihotra — the fire-offering into the breaths

definitions.definition: The first morsels of every meal are offered with 'svāhā' to prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, samāna and udāna, satisfying in turn the senses, their deities and regions; one who eats knowing this offers in all worlds and all selves and his evils burn up like a reed-tuft in fire (ChU 5.19–24); the mantras 'in faith, entered into the breath, I offer the immortal' frame the meal (TA 10.69–70); the whole body becomes the sacrificial ground (Prāṇāgnihotra Up.).
Prescribed in the Dharmasūtra rules for eating as the daily rite of the twice-born at meals.

name: Prāṇa (breath) in the Brāhmaṇas and Āraṇyakas

definitions.definition: The breaths are the primordial seers who made the one Person, Prajāpati (ŚB 6.1.1.1); breath is the consecrated (KB 7.1); the one god is the breath (ŚB 11.6.3); in sleep the breaths enter the self (ŚB 10.5.2.20); the Ṛgvedic seers are forms of the breath (AA 2.2.1); the breaths are counted as five (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna) and sometimes as seven in the head.
Speech was Prajāpati's own and his second, which he sent forth to pervade all (PB 20.14.2); speech is the consecration (KB 7.1); correct speech distinguishes gods from Asuras (ŚB 3.2.1.23–24).
The grammarians read the 'four horns' verse as speech, 'the great god who entered mortals', identity with whom grammar aims at (Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśā).

name: Mind and speech — the two tracks of the sacrifice

definitions.definition: Mind and speech are a yoked pair carrying the sacrifice, mind the greater (ŚB 1.4.4.7); the sacrifice has two tracks, mind (the silent brahman priest) and speech (the other priests) (ChU 4.16.1–2; AB 5.33); in the inner Agnihotra speech and breath are offered into each other (KU 2.5).

name: Parokṣa — the gods' love of the hidden

definitions.definition: 'The gods love the cryptic and dislike the obvious': ritual and cosmic realities are given indirect names (indha → Indra; svāpyaya → svapna), and the teaching of correspondences is itself 'secret' (ŚB 10.5.2.20; 14.6.11.2; AB 3.43).

name: Truth and untruth — gods and men

definitions.definition: The world is twofold — truth and untruth; gods are truth, men untruth; by the vow one passes from untruth to truth, from men to the gods, and must then speak only truth (ŚB 1.1.1.4–5).

Both born of Prajāpati, they contend over the worlds; the Asuras offer into their own mouths in pride, the gods into one another's, and so win the sacrifice (ŚB 5.1.1.1–2); the Asuras lose by barbarous speech (ŚB 3.2.1.23–24) and receive darkness and illusion from Prajāpati (ŚB 2.4.2.5).
The consecrated sacrificer is made an embryo again, the hut his womb, his garments the membranes; he is born at the final bath (AB 1.3); by consecration he makes his future world (ŚB 6.2.2.27).
Consecration for sacrifice is the twice-born's third birth, after the mother and initiation (MDh 2.169).

relations.note: both rites are conceived as births

name: 'A man is born into the world he has made'

definitions.definition: The rites performed (and the knowledge held) here construct the sacrificer's world hereafter (ŚB 6.2.2.27); as one's resolve at death, so one becomes (ŚB 10.6.3.1).
Those who lack the knowledge or the rite are 'born again and again as Death's food' and die again in the other world; the fire-altar and the Nāciketa fire conquer re-death (ŚB 10.4.3; TB 3.11.8).

relations.note: the Brāhmaṇa fear of repeated death is developed in the later doctrine of rebirth by action

name: The weighing of deeds after death

definitions.definition: In the other world a man is placed on a balance and follows whichever side prevails, good or evil; the knower mounts the balance here and escapes it there (ŚB 11.2.7.33); Bhṛgu sees retribution in kind (ŚB 11.6.1; JB 1.42–44).

Śāṇḍilya's meditation: the person is made of resolve; meditate on the self as made of mind, with breath for body, of the form of light, like a grain of rice within yet greater than sky and earth, and resolve to attain it at death (ŚB 10.6.3).
The Chāndogya version adds 'all this is Brahman' and 'this self within the heart is Brahman' (ChU 3.14).

Brahman is the sacred formulation and Veda, and also the first principle: 'in the beginning this was Brahman', which descended into the worlds by name and form (ŚB 11.2.3); 'Brahman the self-existent' heads the teacher-lineages (ŚB 10.6.5.9), offers itself into all beings (ŚB 13.7.1.1), and as a 'great wonder' creates a second god from itself (GB 1.1.1).

name: Creation accounts of the Brāhmaṇas

definitions.definition: Several coexisting accounts: the waters and the golden egg with Prajāpati's first words (ŚB 11.1.6); non-being as the breath-seers (ŚB 6.1.1); neither being nor non-being but mind (ŚB 10.5.3); Prajāpati as boar raising the earth (TB 1.1.3), as tortoise (ŚB 7.5.1.5); the dwarf Viṣṇu (ŚB 1.2.5); the fish and the flood (ŚB 1.8.1); worlds, lights, Vedas, utterances and Oṃ (AB 5.32).

notes: The boar, tortoise, fish and dwarf appear here before their later Purāṇic form as avatāras (U07).

definitions.definition: Formal question-and-answer contests on the hidden meaning of rite and cosmos, with a wager and sometimes deadly stakes (ŚB 11.6.3; 11.4.1).

name: The wind-girdled seers (vātaraśana ṛṣayaḥ)

definitions.definition: Ascetic seers called śramaṇas who kept their seed drawn upward and were found by the other seers through faith and austerity (TA 2.7.1).

notes: Related to the long-haired sage of RV 10.136 (U01).

definitions.definition: Lists at the ends of Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka sections naming the teachers from whom a teaching was received, traced back through seers and gods to Prajāpati and Brahman the self-existent (ŚB 10.6.5.9; 14.9.4.33; Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa; JUB).

name: Gradation of the manifest self (plant, animal, man)

definitions.definition: The self is increasingly manifest from plants (sap) to animals (thought) to man, who has the most intelligence, knows tomorrow and seeks the immortal through the mortal (AA 2.3.2).

name: The secret teaching of the saṃhitā (continuous recitation)

definitions.definition: Meditations that read the joining of words in recitation as the joining of earth and sky, teacher and pupil, mother and father (AA 3.1.1; TU 1.3), assign phoneme-classes to worlds, gods and senses (AA 3.2.5), and explain 'saṃhitā' as Prajāpati putting himself together with the metres (AA 3.2.6).

name: The six limbs of the Veda

definitions.definition: Phonetics, ritual procedure, grammar, etymology, metre and time-reckoning; the Veda's nose, hands, mouth, ear, feet and eye (PŚ 41–42), studied as a duty without motive (Mahābhāṣya); compiled by later seers for ease of learning (Nirukta 1.20); among the fourteen seats of knowledge (YS 1.3); counted as lower knowledge (MuU 1.1.5).
The Vedas and the Vedāṅgas are 'lower knowledge'; the higher is that by which the imperishable is attained (MuU 1.1.4–5) — the Vedāṅga tradition's own placement of itself below realization.
Correspondingly, self-knowledge is 'the foremost of all sciences' (MDh 12.85).

The Veda is kept by exact oral transmission from teacher to pupil in several parallel recitations (continuous, word-by-word, step and the eight 'modified' ones), with attention to accent and quantity; reading from a written text is a fault (PŚ 32); memorization without understanding is 'dry fuel without fire' (Nirukta 1.18); the Vedas are endless (TB 3.10.11).

The three accents (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.29–31) carry meaning and efficacy: Tvaṣṭṛ's mis-accented 'indraśatru' made Indra the slayer (ŚB 1.6.3.10), and a mantra faulty in accent is a thunderbolt against the sacrificer (PŚ 52).
Phoneme (varṇa), accent (svara), quantity (mātrā), force (bala), evenness (sāma) and connection (santāna) (TU 1.2).

Sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes declared by Svayambhū (PŚ 3), produced at eight places (PŚ 13); vowels are selves of Indra, sibilants of Prajāpati, stops of Death (ChU 2.22.3); stops, sibilants and vowels correspond to earth, atmosphere and sky (AA 3.2.5).

name: How speech arises in the body

definitions.definition: The self grasps meanings with the intellect and joins the mind to the wish to speak; the mind strikes the body's fire, which drives the wind up from the chest to the head and mouth, where the phonemes are formed (PŚ 6–9).

relations.note: the Śikṣā's physiology of breath serves pronunciation, not meditation

definitions.definition: Pāṇini received the list of phonemes from Maheśvara (PŚ 56–57); Śiva sounded the fourteen sūtras on his drum at the end of his dance (Nandikeśvara-kāśikā); Bṛhaspati taught Indra words for a thousand divine years (Mahābhāṣya).

Protection of the Veda, adaptation of mantras, obedience to the scriptural command, brevity and removal of doubt; avoiding barbarous speech; the merit of a single well-used word (Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśā and on 6.1.84).

name: Word, meaning and their relation as established (siddha)

definitions.definition: Kātyāyana's first vārttika: word, meaning and relation are established (eternal, per Patañjali); grammar only restricts usage for the sake of dharma; the word is that by which the meaning is understood (Mahābhāṣya).

notes: The fuller philosophy of language (sphoṭa, śabda-brahman) belongs to lin:vyakarana (U31).

definitions.definition: Noun, verb, preverb and particle (Nirukta 1.1); the verb signifies becoming, the noun being.
The same four read into the 'four horns' of RV 4.58.3 (Mahābhāṣya).

name: The six modifications of being (ṣaḍ bhāvavikārāḥ)

definitions.definition: According to Vārṣyāyaṇi, everything that becomes is born, exists, changes, grows, declines and perishes (Nirukta 1.2).

notes: Later Vedānta uses the list for what the unchanging self is free of.

definitions.definition: Śākaṭāyana and the Nairuktas hold that all nouns derive from verbs; Gārgya and some grammarians deny it; Yāska defends derivation, always attending to meaning (Nirukta 1.12; 2.1).

Against Kautsa's claim that mantras are meaningless, Yāska holds they are meaningful because their words are those of ordinary speech; the one who recites without understanding is a load-bearing post (Nirukta 1.15–18).

name: The seer (ṛṣi) as one who saw

definitions.definition: A ṛṣi is so called from seeing the hymns; Brahman the self-existent came upon the seers in their austerity; they had direct vision of dharma (Nirukta 2.11; 1.20).
Seers are no longer born because of transgression, yet some become 'seers by learning' through residual merit (ĀpDh 1.2.5.5).
There are only three deities by station — Agni, Vāyu/Indra, Sūrya (Nirukta 7.5) — and because of the deity's majesty the one self is praised in many ways, the other gods being its limbs (7.4).

relations.note: both name one self behind many names (Nirukta 7.4; MDh 12.123)

definitions.definition: Verses addressed indirectly, directly, or spoken of oneself (ādhyātmika) (Nirukta 7.1).

name: Schools of Vedic interpretation in the Nirukta

definitions.definition: Yāska reports competing readings of the same deity: the etymologists (natural phenomena), the legend-tellers (persons of old stories), the ritualists, and others (Nirukta 2.16; 12.1; 12.10).

Metres defined by syllable count and feet — gāyatrī (24), uṣṇih (28), anuṣṭubh (32), bṛhatī (36), paṅkti (40), triṣṭubh (44), jagatī (48) — described by Piṅgala with light/heavy syllables and three-syllable groups; the gods covered themselves with them against death (ChU 1.4.2); in the Brāhmaṇas each metre corresponds to a god, a class, a season and an animal (TS 7.1.1.4–6).

name: The five-year cycle of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa

definitions.definition: A cycle of five years (saṃvatsara, parivatsara, idāvatsara, anuvatsara, idvatsara) under Prajāpati, beginning with sun and moon together at Śraviṣṭhā in Māgha, with intercalary months to reconcile lunar and solar time.

notes: Names of the five years from memory (moderate).

name: Time as the condition of the sacrifice

definitions.definition: The Vedas exist for the sacrifices, which are enjoined for fixed times; hence the science of time is needed and stands at the head of the limbs (VJ Ṛk 3, 35; Yajus 3); fires are set up under the Kṛttikās because they keep to the east (ŚB 2.1.2.3).
'Veda is the name for mantra and brāhmaṇa'; Brāhmaṇas are injunctions, the rest explanatory statement (ĀpŚS 24.1.30–33).
The Śrauta rites are for human beings able to undertake them, excluding the maimed, the unlearned, eunuchs and śūdras; for the three higher classes, and for women too (KŚS 1.1.1–8).

name: The four Upavedas

definitions.definition: Sciences attached to the four Vedas: medicine (āyurveda), archery/warfare (dhanurveda), music (gāndharvaveda) and statecraft or architecture (arthaśāstra / sthāpatyaveda), as listed in the Caraṇavyūha.

notes: Assignments vary between sources; not verified here.

definitions.definition: The four Vedas, six Vedāṅgas, Purāṇa, nyāya, mīmāṃsā and dharmaśāstra (YS 1.3).
Kauṭilya's fourfold division of sciences — investigation (Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Lokāyata), the triple Veda, economics, governance (Arthaśāstra 1.2).

The Veda, the smṛti and conduct of those who know it, the practice of the good, and what satisfies oneself (MDh 2.6, 2.12); with desire born of right intention (YS 1.7); where texts are silent, the agreement of the knowers and of a learned assembly (ĀpDh 1.1.1.2; MDh 12.108–113); dharma is what the Āryas praise (ĀpDh 1.7.20.6–7); the rest may be learned from women and all classes (ĀpDh 2.11.29.15).

The learned, free of envy, pride and greed (BDh 1.1.1.5), free of desire (VDh 1.6), whose practice is authoritative where the Veda is silent; a single Veda-knower's decision outweighs myriads of the ignorant (MDh 12.113).

name: The authority of regional, caste and family custom

definitions.definition: Customs of regions, castes and families are authoritative when not contrary to the Veda (GDh 11.20); marriage follows local custom (ĀśGS 1.7.1); whether southern and northern practices that the cultured reject are valid is debated (BDh 1.1.2.1–8).

Brahmāvarta between the Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī, the land of the brahmarṣis, Madhyadeśa and Āryāvarta between the mountains and seas; the land of the black antelope is fit for sacrifice (MDh 2.17–24; VDh 1.8–12; YS 1.2).

name: Varṇa — the four classes, as the tradition states it

definitions.definition: The Brāhmaṇas correlate the classes with Prajāpati's limbs, metres, gods and animals, declaring the śūdra unfit for sacrifice (TS 7.1.1.4–6), with the three Vedas (TB 3.12.9.2), and call learned brāhmaṇas 'human gods' (ŚB 2.2.2.6).

Four classes, three of them twice-born (MDh 10.4), created from the mouth, arms, thighs and feet (MDh 1.31), with duties — teaching and sacrificing; protecting; trade and farming; service (MDh 1.88–91); each earlier class superior by birth (ĀpDh 1.1.1.4–8); a lower class rises and a higher falls in the next birth by conduct (ĀpDh 2.5.11.10–11); a brāhmaṇa who neglects the Veda sinks to a śūdra's state (MDh 2.168); penalties for a śūdra hearing the Veda (GDh 12.4–6).

notes: Recorded faithfully as the Brāhmaṇa and Dharmaśāstra traditions state it; the bhakti, Siddha, Buddhist, Jain and Upaniṣadic critiques are recorded by other units and in dsp:women-caste-liberation.

definitions.definition: Offspring of unions across classes form further birth-groups (jāti) — 'with the grain' (anuloma) or 'against the grain' (pratiloma) — each with its occupation; lineages may rise or fall in status over seven generations of marriage (MDh 10.5–65).

The duty of one's class and stage, better imperfect than another's done well (MDh 10.97); each class's work is its austerity (MDh 11.235); following it brings heaven and endlessness (Arthaśāstra 1.3.14) and a good rebirth (ĀpDh 2.1.2.2–3).
When livelihood by one's own duty fails, one may live by the next class's means (with limits), as set out in MDh 10.81ff. — though living permanently by another's dharma causes a fall (MDh 10.97).
Non-injury, truth, not stealing, purity and sense-restraint for all four classes (MDh 10.63), with giving, self-control, compassion and patience (YS 1.122); the Arthaśāstra's list for all (1.3.13).

relations.note: both are class-independent lists of virtues (MDh 6.92; 10.63)

definitions.definition: Steadfastness, patience, self-control, not stealing, purity, sense-restraint, wisdom, learning, truth, absence of anger (MDh 6.92).

name: The aims of human life (puruṣārtha)

definitions.definition: Dharma, artha and kāma, whose combination is the good (MDh 2.224), with mokṣa sought after the debts are paid (MDh 6.35–37); dharmaśāstra prevails over arthaśāstra in conflict (YS 2.21).
Artha is foremost, dharma and kāma being rooted in it (Arthaśāstra 1.7.6–7).
The three pursued over a hundred-year life without mutual harm; dharma, artha, kāma in descending weight; mokṣa in old age (Kāmasūtra 1.2).

notes: The early texts speak of three aims (trivarga); mokṣa as a fourth aim (caturvarga) is systematized later.

definitions.definition: A brāhmaṇa is born owing studentship to the seers, sacrifice to the gods and offspring to the ancestors (TS 6.3.10.5); ŚB adds hospitality to men (1.7.2.1–6).
The debts must be paid before seeking liberation (MDh 6.35–37).
To beings (bali), men (hospitality), ancestors (svadhā), gods (svāhā) and Brahman (self-study) (ŚB 11.5.6.1–3; TA 2.10).
The householder's daily expiation of the five slaughter-places: teaching/study, water-offering, fire-offering, bali, honouring guests (MDh 3.68–70).

Student, householder, forest-hermit and renouncer (MDh 6.87); in sequence they lead to the highest state (MDh 6.88) with the householder as their support and best (MDh 3.77–78; 6.89–90); some allow free choice after studentship (GDh 3.1; VDh 7.3), 'the teachers' recognize only the householder (GDh 3.36; BDh 2.6.11.27), and Āpastamba lists them with his own order (householder first) while criticizing liberation by knowledge alone (ĀpDh 2.9.21).

name: The sacraments (saṃskāra)

definitions.definition: Rites that purify the body from conception to death and make it 'fit for Brahman' (MDh 2.26–28); Gautama's forty, including the daily great sacrifices and the solemn rites, are of no avail without the eight virtues of the self (GDh 8.14–25); later works fix a list of sixteen from conception to cremation.

notes: The sixteen-fold list is the common later one (it varies between texts); Gautama's forty are given in cpt:forty-samskaras-eight-virtues.

name: Gautama's forty sacraments and eight virtues

definitions.definition: Forty sacraments (8 bodily rites, 4 Vedic vows, final bath, marriage, 5 great sacrifices, 7 cooked-food, 7 oblation and 7 Soma sacrifices) and eight virtues of the self (compassion, patience, freedom from envy, purity, calm, auspiciousness, generosity, freedom from greed); the virtues, not the sacraments, decide union with Brahman (GDh 8.14–25).
The teacher becomes pregnant with the pupil and brings him forth with the Sāvitrī on the third night (ŚB 11.5.4.12).
The Vedic birth in which the Sāvitrī is mother and the teacher father (MDh 2.170); the best birth, given by knowledge (ĀpDh 1.1.1.16–17); due at eight, eleven or twelve (MDh 2.36; ĀśGS 1.19).
The student brings fuel and begs daily, so Death has no claim on him (ŚB 11.3.3).

The teacher is revered above the father as giver of the Vedic birth (MDh 2.145–146); learning, not age, makes one great (2.154); the serving pupil obtains the teacher's knowledge as a digger reaches water (2.218); knowledge may be received from anyone in faith (2.238); the ācārya is the one from whom the dharmas are gathered, never to be harmed (ĀpDh 1.1.1.14–15).

name: Fitness of the student and the secrecy of knowledge

definitions.definition: Etymology is not to be taught to one ignorant of grammar, not a pupil, or incapable (Nirukta 2.3–4).
Knowledge asks to be guarded as a treasure, not given to the scornful or crooked; better to die with it than sow it in barren soil (MDh 2.113–115; VDh 2.8–9).
Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, Gautama, Śātātapa, Vasiṣṭha (YS 1.4–5).
Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Prājāpatya, Āsura, Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, Paiśāca (MDh 3.21).

name: Women's dharma (strīdharma), as the tradition states it

definitions.definition: Women are to be honoured, for where they are not all rites fail (MDh 3.56); a woman is to be under the protection of father, husband and sons (MDh 5.148; 9.3); a widow chooses chastity or (in some later texts) ascending the pyre (Viṣṇusmṛti 25.14); women are qualified for Śrauta rites with their husbands (KŚS 1.1.7); dharma may be learned from women (ĀpDh 2.11.29.15); an older tradition distinguishes women who study the Veda (brahmavādinī) from those who marry directly (sadyovadhū) (Hārīta, quoted).

notes: Recorded as stated in the texts; the Hārīta quotation is known only through later digests.

definitions.definition: Purifiers include knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, wind, rites, sun and time; purity in wealth is highest; the mind is purified by truth, the self by knowledge and austerity (MDh 5.105–109).
Relatives within the sapiṇḍa circle are impure for ten days after a death (MDh 5.59) or for periods graded by class (5.83); infants under two are buried without water-offerings (MDh 5.68; YS 3.1).
The āhitāgni is burned with his own fires and implements (ŚB 12.5.2); a funeral mound is later built (ŚB 13.8); the funeral mantras are collected in TA 6.
Cremation with the Yama hymn, burial of infants, water-offerings, bone-collection, ten days' impurity, the first-year offerings and the uniting with the ancestors (ĀśGS 4.1–6; YS 3.1–2; MDh 5.59–68).
The ancestors eat monthly, drink svadhā and have the moon as light (ŚB 2.4.2.2); the paths of the fathers lead to cremation grounds for those who desired offspring (ĀpDh 2.9.23).
Primeval deities of several classes, satisfied by śrāddha offerings for months or forever (MDh 3.192–199; 3.267–272).

name: From the departed (preta) to ancestor (pitṛ)

definitions.definition: The newly dead remains a preta nourished by the rites of the first days and the monthly offerings of the first year, until the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa unites him with father, grandfather and great-grandfather, the most distant then passing out of the piṇḍa circle.

notes: Doctrine stated from the Gṛhya/Dharmaśāstra tradition at large; specific verse anchors to be added in Phase D (Garuḍa Purāṇa → U07).

name: The body for torment after death

definitions.definition: For evil-doers another body arises after death from the five subtle elements, in which they suffer Yama's torments, then dissolves (MDh 12.16–22).

name: Karma of mind, speech and body

definitions.definition: Ten wrongs — three mental, four verbal, three bodily — with mind as instigator; bodily faults lead to plant-births, verbal to bird and beast births, mental to low human births (MDh 12.3–9); the residue of deeds shapes birth, form and fortune (ĀpDh 2.1.2.3); one's own conduct raises or lowers class in the next birth (ĀpDh 2.5.11.10–11).
Sattva (knowledge), rajas (attraction and aversion), tamas (ignorance) as qualities of the self determining whether one goes to the state of gods, men or animals, each in three grades (MDh 12.24–51).

Pravṛtta action, done with desire, leads to prosperity and the gods' state; nivṛtta action, desireless and preceded by knowledge, leads beyond the elements (MDh 12.88–90); abstention bears great fruit (MDh 5.56).

Sins — omission, commission, attachment — are removed by confession, remorse, austerity, recitation and gifts (MDh 11.44, 11.227–229), by japa, tapas, offering, fasting and giving and by purifying texts (GDh 19.11–12); sins are graded from the five great sins down (MDh 11.54ff.).

Dharma declines by a quarter in each age and its chief form changes — austerity, knowledge, sacrifice, giving (MDh 1.81–86); each age has its code — Manu, Gautama, Śaṅkha-Likhita, Parāśara (Parāśarasmṛti 1.24); litigation arose with that decline (Nāradasmṛti Mātṛkā 1.1–2); later authorities list practices forbidden in Kali (kalivarjya).

name: The ages, the Manu-periods and the day of Brahmā

definitions.definition: Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, Kali of 4,000, 3,000, 2,000, 1,000 divine years with twilights; 12,000 make a divine age; a thousand divine ages a day of Brahmā; seventy-one a Manu-period; creations and dissolutions without number (MDh 1.68–80).
The age-names appear in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa as states of a man — lying, rising, standing, moving (AB 7.15).

The self is to be seen by yoga (YS 1.8), is its own witness (MDh 8.84), is distinguished as knower of the field, elemental self and jīva (MDh 12.12–13), is one in all like space in pots or the sun in waters (YS 3.144), and is the one called Agni, Manu, Prajāpati, Indra, breath and Brahman (MDh 12.123); self-knowledge is highest (MDh 12.85); nothing is higher than attaining the self (ĀpDh 1.8.22.2).
The self is its own witness and refuge; the gods and the person within see the evil-doer (MDh 8.84–86).
Five of knowledge, five of action and mind as the eleventh, of both natures (MDh 2.89–92).

Breath-control with Oṃ and the utterances, fixation, withdrawal and meditation burn away faults, sin, attachment and ungodly qualities (MDh 6.70–74); the removal of the fifteen faults is rooted in yoga (ĀpDh 1.8.23); seeing the self by yoga is the highest dharma (YS 1.8); the Yājñavalkyasmṛti describes yogic powers (3.202–203) and liberation through music (3.115).
